title: 'This Fund Is Not Managed': John Bogle's First Index Fund, 1975
dek: Fired from Wellington and left with a company barred from managing money, Bogle proposed a fund that needed no manager.

story.event: Proposing and launching the first index mutual fund inside Vanguard's narrow charter
story.summary: Fired as chief executive of Wellington Management in January 1974, John Bogle stayed on as chairman of the Wellington funds, whose board created Vanguard to administer them but barred it from investment management. In September 1975 he persuaded the board to approve an index fund on the grounds that it was not managed. The 1976 underwriting raised about $11 million against hopes of up to $150 million; Bogle refused to return the money, and First Index Investment Trust opened on 31 August 1976.
paragraphs: On 23 January 1974, John Bogle was fired as chief executive of Wellington Management Company, after the 1966 merger that had brought in new partners went sour. "My new partners ganged up and fired me," he said later. The next day the board of the Wellington funds, largely independent of the management company, met in New York. Bogle was still the funds' chairman. He urged the directors to run the funds themselves; they would only let him study the options.

In September 1974 they chose the option he had ranked last. A new company, which he named Vanguard, would run the funds' administration, while Wellington kept investment management and selling. Vanguard began work on 1 May 1975. Bogle saw a gap in that narrow charter: a fund that simply held the stocks of the S&P 500 needed no manager. His 1951 Princeton thesis had concluded that funds could make no claim to beat the market indexes, and Paul Samuelson's 1974 essay "Challenge to Judgment" had all but asked for such a fund.

Over the summer of 1975, with two young colleagues, Jim Riepe and Jan Twardowski, he built the case. Working on a mechanical calculator, he found that from 1945 to 1975 the average fund had returned 9.7 per cent a year, against 11.3 per cent for the index. "This fund is not managed," he told the directors. Most of their discussion was about whether it fitted Vanguard's mandate, and in September 1975 they approved it.

Raising the money was harder. Stocks had nearly halved in 1973 and 1974, and on road shows in a dozen cities the brokers were cool on a fund implying that picking managers was a loser's game. Bogle had told his board he hoped for $50 million to $150 million. The offering raised about $11 million, and the underwriters wanted to give it back. "I said, 'Hell no,'" Bogle recalled. First Index Investment Trust opened on 31 August 1976.

In February 1977, by eight votes to five, the directors let Vanguard sell its funds itself, without sales charges. The index fund had no mutual fund competitor until 1984. It is now the Vanguard 500 Index Fund.

quote.text: One of the vizirs was displaced, and withdrew into a fraternity of dervishes, whose blessed society made its impression upon him and afforded consolation to his mind.
quote.locator: Chapter I, "Of the Customs of Kings", Story XV
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi's displaced vizier found consolation out of office and, in the rest of the story, turned down the king's offer to take him back. Bogle, fired one day, was in front of a board the next, fighting for the job. Saadi does not say which of them chose more wisely, and neither does this story.

reflection: Bogle's story is usually told as a comeback, and it was one. But its shape is narrower than the legend: a dismissal he did not want, a charter that barred him from the work he knew best, and a launch that raised a fraction of its target. He worked inside each limit instead of waiting for it to lift.

Saadi's vizier offers the other path, and it deserves a hearing. Not every closed door is a puzzle to solve. When something in your work is taken away or made smaller, you are allowed to ask first whether you actually want it back.
invitation: Name one limit you are working under this month. Before you push against it, write one line on whether you truly want what lies on the other side of it.

cross_checks.claim: Bogle was fired as chief executive of Wellington Management in January 1974, and the new Vanguard was confined to administration, not investment management
In September 1975 the board approved the index fund after Bogle argued that it involved no investment management
The 1976 underwriting raised about $11 million, far short of the target
First Index Investment Trust began operations on 31 August 1976

research_notes: Bogle told this story several times and his own accounts differ. Board meeting: 18 September 1975 in his 1997 history, 27 September 1975 in his 2017 remarks; the story says September 1975. Amount raised: $11.4 million (1997) and $11.3 million (2017 remarks; Zweig 2016); the story says about $11 million. Target: his 1997 history quotes his letter to the board, 'in the $50 million to $150 million range', and elsewhere calls $150 million the initial objective (as does Zweig); his 2017 remarks say the offering was planned for $250 million. The story uses the contemporary board-letter range. Board vote: the 2017 remarks call the approval unanimous, while Zweig (interviewing Bogle in 2016) reports one director voted for it but refused to join the fund's board, and that directors approved partly because they were tired of his pressing; the story says only that they approved it. The 1945-1975 return figures (9.7 and 11.3 per cent, a 1.6-point gap) are from the 1997 history; the 2017 remarks give the same 1.6-point edge and say he worked it out on a Monroe mechanical calculator. Bogle's 2017 remarks say the merger 'collapsed in 1974' and that his 'new partners' fired him; the story does not assign further blame. The 2017 PDF loads but the checker cannot read its compressed text, so it shows as live without a name match. Funding is 'mixed': Vanguard was owned by the funds it served, and the fund's capital came from a public brokers' underwriting. The New York Times obituary and Morningstar's 2026 retrospective were blocked (403) and are not cited. Quote: the Saadi passage is the opening of the story in which the displaced vizier later declines reinstatement; the connection describes the rest of the story.
